SK2103 The attribute is applied twice with the same arguments

One declaration carries the same AllowMultiple attribute more than once with provably identical arguments, so nothing distinguishes the second application from the first.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since1.3

Why

⚠ This is the one of issue #269's four sub-concepts the compiler is silent about, and the silence is the point. An attribute applied to a target it does not declare is CS0592; applied twice when AllowMultiple is false it is CS0579; naming a member that does not exist it is CS8776 for the nullable-contract attributes and SK2102 for [DebuggerDisplay]. For an AllowMultiple attribute the repetition is legal — it is simply indistinguishable from writing it once — so it survives review, and what it costs depends on who reads the metadata: a duplicated [InlineData] runs one test case twice under a name that says it ran once, and a duplicated [SuppressMessage] is dead metadata that the next person tries to work out the difference between.

Example

Instead of:

[Conditional("TRACE")]
[Conditional("TRACE")]
static void Log(string message) { }

Write:

[Conditional("TRACE")]
static void Log(string message) { }

When it does not fire

⚠ Identity is proved, never assumed. If any argument on either application is not a compile-time constant or a typeof, the pair is declined: two expressions that might differ are not a repetition. Positional arguments are compared in order and named ones by name; a name: argument makes position and name two different orderings of one list and declines the pair rather than guessing. ⚠ Only an attribute whose `AttributeUsage` reaches `AllowMultiple = true` is considered — anything else cannot legally repeat, so a second application is CS0579 and this rule has nothing to add to source that does not compile. The AttributeUsage lookup walks the attribute class's base chain, because that is what the runtime's own lookup does. ⚠ `[method: X]` and `[return: X]` are two different things written on one declaration, so the target is part of the group's identity and the two never compare against each other. ⚠ Attribute lists on two `partial` declarations of one type are not compared: the repetition is real but it is spread across files, the repair is a judgement about which file keeps it, and the answer would stop being decidable from the file the finding is in — which is what scope: Semantic promises the cache. Assembly-level lists are compared within one file for the same reason. The finding lands on the second and later applications, never the first, and the fix deletes that one application together with whichever separator it needs so the list still parses.
